strengths: The paper addresses an important continual segmentation problem by combining class-balanced contrastive learning, retained class prototypes, and learned assignment to multiple unknown clusters. This is a potentially useful extension beyond representing all future classes with one background prototype.

The reported empirical gains are broad and include comparisons using the same segmentation architecture. With DeepLab-V3, FALCON achieves 36.4 versus 34.9 mIoU for RCIL+LGKD on ADE20K 100-10, 62.41 versus 59.25 for SSUL on VOC 10-1, and 55.24 versus 49.22 for FairCL on Cityscapes 1-1. Experiments with transformer backbones further support applicability across architectures.

The ablations provide meaningful positive evidence. Table 1 improves minority-class mIoU from 26.4 to 30.8 and from 24.9 to 28.7 without sacrificing majority-class performance. Table 4 supports adapting the visual-grammar model, while supplementary experiments examine sensitivity to cluster margin, neighborhood size, and backbone.
weaknesses: The central fairness argument does not establish its claimed geometric interpretation. Propositions 1–2 characterize normalized probability allocation, but smaller softmax probabilities do not imply more compact clusters. Feature components orthogonal to a centroid can change cluster spread without changing these probabilities. Consequently, reducing probability differences across class sizes does not establish reduced class bias, although the empirical minority-class improvements remain valuable.

The specified objective has consequential ambiguities. Proposition 2 requires the transition vector v to participate in the common softmax normalization, but Eq. (4) retains the feature normalizer from Eq. (2) without specifying this inclusion. With a feature-only denominator and unconstrained v, the objective is unbounded below. Furthermore, Eq. (8) optimizes network parameters while its regularizer depends only on frozen or periodically momentum-updated centroids; no gradient path or separate optimization step explains the regularizer's reported benefit in Table 3. These issues leave uncertainty about the objective actually evaluated.

The supplementary connection to knowledge distillation is not valid as presented. Eqs. (16)–(17) invoke a metric triangle inequality and identify its distance term with the contrastive objective, without establishing that this objective satisfies metric properties. The subsequent Big-O manipulation therefore does not justify the claimed distillation upper bound or preservation guarantee.

Some ablations do not isolate the proposed mechanisms. Table 1 simultaneously introduces v and rescales the feature contrastive term by alpha; a weight-matched vanilla objective is needed to distinguish rebalancing from changing regularization strength. The ablation without visual grammar also switches to a single unknown cluster, confounding assignment quality with cluster multiplicity. Figure 6 provides qualitative support for unknown-class separation, but quantitative assignment or clustering quality is not reported.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful optimizer and memory-update details. The manuscript does not adequately specify DBSCAN parameters, how unknown pixels are selected from background containing old classes, the visual-grammar pretraining procedure and training duration, or the exact majority/minority partition. The broad empirical results are worthwhile, but the unresolved central formulation, theoretical justification, and implementation details currently favor weak rejection.
